title: Privilege Log Review and Clawback Analysis — Deficiency Memo and Clawback Candidate List

blind.coverage: Read all 82 criteria, the one-sentence instructions, the solver system prompt (it says nothing about spreadsheet columns, risk tiers, or required citations) and the judge prompt (it asks whether output 'satisfies the criterion as described', so the 'because X' rationale in a PASS clause is likely enforced). Parsed all 312 privilege-log rows. Read in full: the org chart, the engagement letter, the Garfield CIA, the expert disclosures, and sample docs 003, 005, 007, 009, 011, 024, 025, 031, 037, 044, 055, 067, 072, 076, 078, 085, 089, 091, 093, 102, 104, 108, 112, 119, 128, 141, 143, 147, 152, 156, 158, 162, 167, 168, 175, 184, 189, 198, 199, 201, 203, 210, 245, 267. Read 177 through its memo and the start of the ops review. For 033/058/096/134, read the headers and grepped for anticipation/litigation/counsel. Searched the Pacific Mutual CIA by keyword only. Grepped every .txt for 'October 1, 2024', 'compel', 'deadline', '2024' and '502'. Primary law read this session: In re Allen, 106 F.3d 582 (4th Cir. 1997); Westinghouse v. Republic of the Philippines, 951 F.2d 1414 (3d Cir. 1991); FRCP 26(b)(4)(B)-(C) and 26(b)(5)(A) (via Cornell LII). I did not read Upjohn directly (only as quoted in Allen). I found no controlling Third Circuit 'dominant purpose' decision in a keyword search, but did not exhaustively confirm. Also noted: the log has unplanted Langford pre-GC entries (#1, #4, #6, #8, #10) and a pre-engagement Marsh entry (#2). No criterion penalizes flagging them, so they are not listed as defects.

findings.title: Required 'October 1, 2024' motion-to-compel response deadline appears nowhere in the record
findings.explanation: C-079 fails any memo that omits an October 1, 2024 deadline for Thornfield's response to a motion to compel. I grepped all 55 supplied documents for 'October 1, 2024', 'compel' and 'deadline'. No motion to compel and no such deadline exist. The only 'October 1' hits are an unrelated 2021 custodian-list request (sample-doc-076) and audit reporting periods. The instructions do not mention it either. The record's posture is also incoherent: log entries describe a 2023 bench trial, post-trial and appellate memos through June 30, 2024, while other documents set discovery cutoff at September 30, 2024. A solver working only from the record cannot satisfy this criterion without inventing a fact.

evidence.quote: PASS if the memo references the October 1, 2024 deadline for Thornfield's response to the motion to compel.
Please provide an updated list of custodians who may have additional responsive documents by end of day Friday, October 1.
Outside counsel's post-trial assessment memorandum analyzing trial out[come]
Given that the discovery cutoff is September 30, 2024

findings.suggested_fix: Delete C-079, or add a motion to compel and its response deadline to the record (or to the instructions).

findings.title: Requires memo to say Upjohn generally does not reach former employees, contrary to the majority rule
findings.explanation: C-056 requires the memo to state that Upjohn 'does not generally extend to former employees, particularly in the Third Circuit where the privilege is narrowly construed'. In re Allen reports the opposite: most courts follow Chief Justice Burger's Upjohn concurrence and extend the privilege to former employees for conduct within their employment. I found no Third Circuit authority construing it narrowly. Brannigan was asked about his 2017-2019 tenure as Plant Manager, the classic majority-rule fact pattern. Counsel's questions also reflect opinion work product. A competent memo that states the correct law (#210 is questionable but likely defensible, or should be re-logged as WP) fails C-056. The criterion rewards a misstatement of law.

evidence.quote: the corporate attorney-client privilege under Upjohn does not generally extend to former employees, particularly in the Third Circuit where the privilege is narrowly construed for former employees
During your tenure as Plant Manager, what protocols were in place for the storage and handling of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)

authorities.proposition: 'Most lower courts have followed the Chief Justice's reasoning and granted the privilege to communications between a client's counsel and the client's former employees'; Upjohn analysis 'applies equally to former employees.'

authorities.citation: Upjohn Co. v. United States, 449 U.S. 383, 394 n.3, 402-03 (1981) (Burger, C.J., concurring)
authorities.proposition: Majority left former-employee question open; concurrence would extend privilege to former employees speaking about conduct within scope of employment (as quoted in Allen).

findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite C-056 to require an analysis of the former-employee issue: Upjohn left it open; most courts extend the privilege to conduct within the scope of former employment; the risk is that Brannigan is outside the corporate client and the communication was sent to a personal email; work product is an alternative basis. Drop the 'narrowly construed in the Third Circuit' claim.

findings.title: C-082's two-way presence test nullifies C-080's five-entry tolerance and penalizes reasoned disagreement
findings.explanation: C-080 passes a list missing up to 5 planted entries. C-082 fails if any planted entry 'appears in one deliverable but is absent from' the other. C-001 to C-063 effectively require the memo to discuss every planted entry, so any entry missing from the spreadsheet fails C-082. C-080's stated tolerance therefore never applies under all-pass. It also fails a memo that correctly discusses an entry but concludes the claim is defensible and leaves it off a 'candidate' list. Examples: #210 under the majority former-employee rule, or #072 where the crime-fraud risk is judged low. A single judgment call becomes an automatic zero.

evidence.quote: Missing 5 or fewer specific entries is still a PASS.
FAIL if any planted-issue entry appears in one deliverable but is absent from or contradicted in the other.

findings.suggested_fix: Limit C-082 to contradictions: an entry flagged deficient in the memo must not be marked defensible in the list, and vice versa. Allow the memo to discuss entries it clears, and keep the list-completeness tolerance in C-080 alone.

findings.title: Mandatory 10-column schema and High/Medium/Low risk tiers are never requested
findings.explanation: The instructions are one sentence: assess defensibility, prepare a 'categorized assessment', output two named files. The solver system prompt adds nothing about structure. C-069 fails the spreadsheet if any of ten named columns is missing, including 'Bates Range', 'Risk Level' and 'Brief Explanation'. C-070 requires a three-tier risk scale. C-072 and C-073 then grade specific tier assignments. A competent list could categorize by deficiency type and recommended action (produce, amend log, withhold, in camera) with no 'risk level', or omit Bates ranges already in the log. That list is a sound work product but fails four criteria. 'Categorized' does not imply these particular columns or a risk scale. C-071 (differentiated recommendations) is implicit and fine.

evidence.quote: Review the attached privilege log and sample documents for defensibility of each privilege claim and prepare a categorized assessment. Output: `deficiency-analysis-memo.docx` and `clawback-candidate-list.xlsx`.
Entry Number, Bates Range, Date, Author, Recipient, Privilege Basis Claimed, Deficiency Category, Risk Level, Recommended Action, Brief Explanation. FAIL if any of these columns are missing.
PASS if the Risk Level column uses High, Medium, and Low designations (or equivalent three-tier system).

findings.suggested_fix: State the required columns and the three-tier risk scale in the instructions, or relax C-069 to 'identifies each entry, the deficiency, and a recommended action' and C-070/C-072/C-073 to 'differentiates severity or strength of claim in some form'.

findings.title: Entry #203 is Molina to the General Counsel, so 'Molina is not a licensed attorney' is the wrong rationale
findings.explanation: C-010 passes only if #203 is flagged 'because Molina is not a licensed attorney'. But sample-doc-203 is Molina writing to Margaret Langford, the General Counsel. The log's 'Communication with counsel' is literally accurate, and a non-lawyer employee's communication to corporate counsel can be privileged under Upjohn. The real defect is content: a business debrief of a meeting with NJDEP (an adversary co-plaintiff) that seeks no legal advice. The judge prompt asks whether output meets the criterion 'as described'. A memo that gives the correct reason and correctly notes Molina's status is irrelevant here risks failing, while an incorrect rationale is rewarded.

evidence.quote: **From:** Teresa Molina, Vice President, Government Relations, Thornfield Industries, Inc. **To:** Margaret Langford, Esq., General Counsel
Communication with counsel re: regulatory strategy and state regulator
PASS if the agent identifies Entry #203 (Molina to Langford, September 12, 2022) as deficient because Molina is not a licensed attorney.

findings.suggested_fix: Accept flagging #203 because it is a business/informational report that seeks no legal advice (and relays statements by an adversary). Do not require the Molina-status rationale for this entry.

findings.title: C-047 embeds an overbroad rule that documents meant for public release 'cannot be work product'
findings.explanation: C-047 passes only if #162 is flagged because 'a document intended for public dissemination cannot be work product', it was not prepared by or for counsel, and it has no litigation nexus. The first proposition is wrong as a categorical rule: drafts of briefs and pleadings meant for public filing are classic work product. The correct reason is the second one: a non-lawyer's press release draft, not prepared at counsel's direction or because of litigation. The third is debatable, since the release discusses the remediation at issue. A careful memo that declines to state the categorical rule may be failed by a judge enforcing the criterion as written.

evidence.quote: because a document intended for public dissemination cannot be work product, it was not prepared by or at the direction of an attorney, and it has no litigation nexus
I'm hoping to distribute this to our standard media contact list and post it simultaneously on the corporate website

findings.suggested_fix: Require the core reasons: author is a non-lawyer communications VP, no counsel direction, prepared for public relations rather than because of litigation. Drop the categorical 'cannot be work product' phrasing.

findings.title: Requires 'Third Circuit dominant purpose test' and a '90%+ business / single sentence' articulation
findings.explanation: The primary/predominant-purpose inquiry for dual-purpose communications is standard. But C-031 names it a 'Third Circuit' test and requires explaining that '90%+' business content with a single legal sentence means business dominance. I found no controlling Third Circuit decision adopting that label. District courts in the circuit commonly say 'primary purpose'. A judge may fail a memo that applies the primary-purpose test correctly without a numeric proportion or Third Circuit attribution. Best practice might also be to redact the one legal sentence rather than withhold or produce the whole email, which the criterion does not contemplate.

evidence.quote: references the Third Circuit's dominant purpose test for dual-purpose communications and explains that when 90%+ of a communication is business and only a single sentence requests legal input

findings.suggested_fix: Accept any correct articulation of the primary/predominant purpose test applied to #044/#119/#156. Drop the quantitative '90%+' requirement and the circuit-specific label.

findings.title: Attributes a three-element log-content rule to Rule 26(b)(5)(A)
findings.explanation: Rule 26(b)(5)(A) requires the party to expressly claim privilege and describe the withheld items so others can assess the claim. The elements C-046 demands (subject matter, attorney involved, nature of advice) are a case-law gloss, not rule text. A memo that accurately quotes the rule and explains why #147, #152 etc. prevent assessment may fail if it does not list those three items.

evidence.quote: privilege logs must identify the subject matter, the attorney involved, and the nature of the advice sought or given

authorities.proposition: Party must '(i) expressly make the claim; and (ii) describe the nature of the documents, communications, or tangible things not produced or disclosed' so as to enable others to assess the claim.

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo explains that log descriptions must give enough information (e.g., author/recipient roles, subject matter, basis) to let the opposing party assess the claim.

findings.title: All three waiver entries must be rated High despite live counterarguments on #078 and #102
findings.explanation: C-072 fails the list if #078, #102 or #128 is rated Medium. #128 (disclosure to an adversary) is clear. #078, however, was forwarded by the VP of EHS against outside counsel's express written instruction. That raises authority-to-waive questions (privilege belongs to the corporation), and the recipient was Thornfield's own consultant, later its testifying expert. For #102 and #078, work product is waived only by disclosure to an adversary or that substantially increases adversary access (Westinghouse). The broker disclosure likely preserves work product that an amended log could assert. A reasoned Medium rating is defensible, and it also depends on the unrequested risk scale (O4).

evidence.quote: Please do not share any internal legal assessments with third parties, including environmental consultants, without first establishing appropriate protections.
FAIL if any waiver entry is rated Medium or Low.

authorities.citation: Westinghouse Elec. Corp. v. Republic of the Philippines, 951 F.2d 1414 (3d Cir. 1991)
authorities.proposition: Rejects selective waiver; disclosure to third parties waives attorney-client privilege unless it serves the purpose of obtaining legal advice (work-product waiver is analyzed separately).

findings.suggested_fix: Require #128 to be highest-tier. Accept High or Medium for #078/#102 if the memo explains the waiver risk.

findings.title: Distractor #025's log date conflicts with its document date, inviting a flag that C-064 penalizes
findings.explanation: C-064 fails any answer that flags #025, #039 or #050 'as having a privilege deficiency'. The log dates #025 April 10, 2020, but sample-doc-025 is dated April 10, 2019. Privilege holds either way, since Langford was GC by March 15, 2019. A diligent reviewer should still note the metadata error and recommend correcting the log, just as C-057/C-058 reward catching impossible dates. Listing #025 in the spreadsheet for log correction could be read by a judge as flagging it deficient.

evidence.quote: 25 | TF-PRIV-000195 – TF-PRIV-000203 | April 10, 2020 | Margaret Langford, Esq. | Donald Pruitt
**Date:** April 10, 2019 **Subject:** Legal Analysis --- New NJDEP Reporting Requirements for PFAS Compounds

findings.suggested_fix: Fix the date on the log or the document. Or clarify in C-064 that noting a metadata or date correction does not count as flagging a privilege deficiency.

findings.title: 'Clawback candidate list' is a misnomer for a list of withheld entries with deficient claims
findings.explanation: In ordinary practice, a clawback list identifies privileged documents that were produced and should be retrieved under FRE 502(b)/(d) or a protective order. The rubric instead treats the spreadsheet as a list of withheld log entries whose privilege claims fail (C-080's 42 entries). Some sample documents carry 'DOCUMENT PRODUCTION' headers, which supports the literal reading. A solver following standard usage could build the opposite list and fail C-069, C-080 and C-082. The memo name 'deficiency-analysis' makes the rubric's reading plausible but not certain.

evidence.quote: **PRINTED EMAIL --- THORNFIELD INDUSTRIES, INC. DOCUMENT PRODUCTION**
**PRINTED EMAIL CORRESPONDENCE --- DOCUMENT PRODUCTION** **Bates Range: TF-PRIV-000616 through TF-PRIV-000618** **Privilege Log Entry #: 078**

findings.suggested_fix: Rename the deliverable (e.g., 'challenged-entries-list.xlsx'), or state in the instructions that it should list log entries whose privilege claims are deficient.

findings.title: Record anachronisms and log/document date mismatches, including an early Reese 'designation'
findings.explanation: sample-doc-184 (March 5, 2022) says Reese 'has been formally designated as a testifying expert', which conflicts with the January 15, 2024 disclosure required by C-078. sample-doc-093 (April 2021) cites fees 'through June 2024'. sample-doc-162 (April 2022) cites FY2023 revenue. Judge names vary: Hayward/Walford, Hillburn, Hillman, Waldor. Many log dates differ from the underlying documents (#093, #104, #108, #147, #152, #168, #175, #189, #201, #245, #267). None of this defeats the graded answers, but it makes the correct Reese chronology contestable and adds unrewarded log-accuracy issues.

evidence.quote: Now that Dr. Reese has been formally designated as a testifying expert for Thornfield
Filed: January 15, 2024
CLM legal fees to date are approximately \$3.1 million through June 2024

findings.suggested_fix: Correct the anachronistic passages and align log dates with document dates, or add criteria that reward catching these log/document discrepancies.

blind.overall: The rubric mostly works: most issue-spotting criteria (C-001 to C-063) rest on facts the record clearly supports, and several legal points hold up on the record or on primary law. The ban on retroactive common-interest protection is backed by Garfield CIA §§2.4, 5.4 and 7.2. The Third Circuit rule against selective waiver is confirmed by Westinghouse. The testifying-expert criteria for #199 are supported because the Rule 26(a)(2) disclosure lists the March 2022 report as material Dr. Reese considered. Five defects are serious enough to zero out a correct answer under all-pass scoring. (1) C-079 requires a motion-to-compel deadline that does not exist in the record. (2) C-056 requires an incorrect statement of the former-employee Upjohn rule. (3) C-082's two-way presence test cancels C-080's tolerance and penalizes a reasoned disagreement with any planted issue. (4) C-069/C-070 impose a column schema and risk tiers the instructions never ask for, and C-072/C-073 grade against those tiers. (5) C-010 builds in the wrong rationale for #203, a message addressed to the General Counsel. Further arguable problems: overbroad legal propositions in C-047 and C-046, the '90%+' framing in C-031, a trap around the #025 date conflict, and the ambiguous 'clawback' label. Taken together, a strong, legally careful answer has a materially reduced chance of passing every criterion.

sol_verdicts.reason: I searched all 55 extracted documents and found no 'October 1, 2024' and no motion to compel with a response deadline. The only 'October 1' is an unrelated 2021 custodian request in sample-doc-076. The instructions do not mention a deadline either. Satisfying C-079 requires inventing a fact.

In re Allen (read this session) says Upjohn left the former-employee question open, 'Most lower courts have followed the Chief Justice's reasoning and granted the privilege' to former employees, and the Upjohn analysis 'applies equally to former employees.' Brannigan was asked about conduct during his tenure as Plant Manager. C-056 requires a memo to state the opposite rule.

Flagging #162 is correct: a non-lawyer's press-release draft with no counsel involvement. But the rationale overstates the law. Rule 26(b)(3)(A) (read this session) covers materials prepared 'by or for another party or its representative', so no attorney is required, and drafts meant for eventual publication are not categorically excluded. A correct memo will naturally recite the same facts (non-lawyer author, PR purpose, no litigation driver), so the risk of misgrading is real but limited.

The log descriptions for #147, 152, 168, 175, 189, 201, 245 and 267 are plainly boilerplate (e.g., 'Legal communication', 'Privileged and confidential'). C-037 to C-044 only require flagging that, and date mismatches with the samples only strengthen the flag. C-064 is different: #025's log date (April 10, 2020) conflicts with its sample (April 10, 2019), so noting that metadata error could be read as flagging a deficiency.

Common-interest protection can exist without a written agreement, but this record forecloses a prior informal arrangement. Garfield CIA §7.2 says 'There are no prior agreements, whether formal or informal, written or oral', and §2.4 bars retroactivity. #085 is an exploratory 'good faith gesture' sent before any arrangement. #091's 'in the interim' language gives a careful memo nuance to discuss, but it does not make flagging #091 or C-027's non-retroactivity statement wrong.

#078 and #102 are logged as ACP only, so ACP waiver defeats the logged basis. Pruitt forwarded under the business MSA against Marsh's express warning, and the Pacific Mutual CIA excludes Ridgeline, so C-020, C-022 and C-023 are sound. But the expert disclosure says Reese has had a 'separate litigation support engagement coordinated through Carrick, Lowe & Marsh LLP' since 2020. That undercuts C-021's 'no privilege protection arrangement' and supports a reasoned Medium rating for #078 under C-072. Work product may also survive.

Flagging #044, #119 and #156 as over-withheld, business-dominant emails is correct, and a redact-and-produce recommendation still counts as flagging. C-031 turns a '90%+/single sentence' ratio and a 'Third Circuit' label into required content. C-073 bans an all-High rating, even though C-031's own framing treats these as clearly business-dominant. It also depends on the unrequested risk scale.

#203 is Molina writing to GC Langford, and the log lists her without 'Esq.', so 'Communication with counsel' is accurate. Her lack of a license is legally irrelevant when the recipient is counsel, and the real defect is the business content of the debrief. C-010 rewards a wrong rationale, so I rate it problematic, not merely arguable. C-011 is directly supported by the org chart note on the informal 'regulatory counsel' title.

The disclosure designates Reese and lists the 'Technical report on contamination migration patterns dated March 22, 2022' as material he considered, so C-062 is well founded. C-063's statement that 'materials considered by the expert lose' protection conflicts with Rule 26(b)(4)(B)-(C) (read this session). Those provisions keep drafts and attorney-expert communications protected except for compensation, facts or data, and assumptions. The overbroad rule is rewarded, though a nuanced memo would usually still pass.

The one-sentence prompt asks only for a 'categorized assessment'. C-069's ten mandatory columns and C-070's three-tier risk scale are hidden. C-082's two-way presence test fails any reasoned clearance of a planted entry and cancels C-080's five-entry tolerance. C-046 attributes a case-law gloss (subject matter, attorney involved, nature of advice) to Rule 26(b)(5)(A). C-080 is fine on its own but depends on the ambiguous 'clawback' label.

In sample-doc-072, Pruitt asks whether there is a 'legal basis for holding off', and Langford warns of significant enforcement risk. Nothing shows delay actually occurred or that the advice was used to further a crime. Seeking advice on legality is core privilege. A memo concluding the exception does not apply risks failing C-052 and C-081. C-053 only describes the conduct at issue if crime-fraud is discussed, and C-054 states the correct standard.

findings.title: Requires memo to say Upjohn generally does not reach former employees, contrary to the majority rule
findings.explanation: C-056 requires stating that Upjohn privilege 'does not generally extend to former employees', narrowly construed in the Third Circuit. Upjohn left the question open. Allen reports that most courts extend the privilege to former employees communicating about conduct within their employment, and that courts denying it usually involved conduct after employment ended. Marsh questioned Brannigan about his tenure as Plant Manager, the classic majority-rule fact pattern. A memo stating the correct law (privilege likely available but contestable, with work product as a fallback) fails C-056.

evidence.quote: the corporate attorney-client privilege under Upjohn does not generally extend to former employees, particularly in the Third Circuit where the privilege is narrowly construed for former employees
During your tenure as Plant Manager, what protocols were in place for the storage and handling of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)

authorities.proposition: 'Most lower courts have followed the Chief Justice's reasoning and granted the privilege to communications between a client's counsel and the client's former employees'; the Upjohn analysis 'applies equally to former employees.'

authorities.citation: Upjohn Co. v. United States, 449 U.S. 383, 394 n.3 (1981); id. at 402-03 (Burger, C.J., concurring)
authorities.proposition: Majority left former-employee question open; concurrence would extend privilege to former employees speaking about conduct within scope of employment (read as quoted in Allen).

findings.suggested_fix: Require analysis of the former-employee issue: Upjohn left it open, most courts protect communications about conduct within the scope of employment, the personal-email and non-agent risks, and work product as an alternative basis. Drop the 'narrowly construed in the Third Circuit' claim.

findings.title: C-082's two-way presence test fails reasoned clearance of any planted entry and nullifies C-080's tolerance
findings.explanation: C-082 fails if any of 42 planted entries 'appears in one deliverable but is absent from' the other. The issue-spotting criteria effectively require the memo to discuss every planted entry. So any entry the memo discusses but reasonably clears is absent from the candidate list, and C-082 fails. Examples: #072 where crime-fraud is judged inapplicable, #210 under the majority former-employee rule, or #078 given Reese's counsel-coordinated engagement. That makes C-080's 'missing 5 or fewer' tolerance meaningless under all-pass scoring, and a single judgment call becomes an automatic zero.

evidence.quote: Missing 5 or fewer specific entries is still a PASS.
FAIL if any planted-issue entry appears in one deliverable but is absent from or contradicted in the other.

findings.suggested_fix: Limit C-082 to real contradictions: an entry found deficient in one deliverable must not be treated as sound in the other. Allow the memo to discuss entries it clears.

findings.title: Mandatory 10-column schema and High/Medium/Low risk tiers are never requested
findings.explanation: The instructions ask only for a 'categorized assessment' in two named files, and the system prompt adds no structure. C-069 fails the spreadsheet if any of ten specified columns is missing, including Bates Range, Risk Level and Brief Explanation. C-070 requires a three-tier risk scale. 'Categorized' naturally means grouped by deficiency type, and a practitioner could reasonably organize by deficiency and recommended action (produce, amend log, redact, in camera) with no risk rating. Such a list is sound work product but fails both criteria. C-071 (differentiated recommendations) is implicit and not flagged.

evidence.quote: Review the attached privilege log and sample documents for defensibility of each privilege claim and prepare a categorized assessment.
FAIL if any of these columns are missing.
PASS if the Risk Level column uses High, Medium, and Low designations (or equivalent three-tier system).

findings.suggested_fix: State the columns and risk scale in the instructions, or relax C-069 and C-070 to require entry identification, deficiency, recommended action and some differentiation of severity.

findings.title: Entry #203 is Molina writing to the General Counsel, so 'Molina is not a licensed attorney' is the wrong rationale
findings.explanation: The other Molina entries (#031, 055, 089, 141) go to non-lawyers but are logged as 'Communication with counsel', so the log implies Molina is counsel. #203 is addressed to GC Langford, so the same description is literally accurate, and a non-lawyer employee's communication to corporate counsel can be privileged. The real defect is content: a business debrief of an NJDEP meeting that seeks no legal advice. C-010 rewards an irrelevant rationale and exposes a correct content-based analysis to failure by a judge enforcing 'because Molina is not a licensed attorney'.

evidence.quote: **From:** Teresa Molina, Vice President, Government Relations, Thornfield Industries, Inc. **To:** Margaret Langford, Esq., General Counsel
D204='Teresa Molina' | E204='Margaret Langford, Esq.'
as deficient because Molina is not a licensed attorney

findings.suggested_fix: For #203, accept flagging on business-purpose grounds: an informational report of a regulator meeting that seeks no legal advice. Do not require the Molina-status rationale.

findings.title: C-047's rationale embeds two overbroad work-product rules (public-dissemination bar; attorney-direction requirement)
findings.explanation: Flagging #162 is correct: VP Communications Stanton drafted a press release with no counsel involvement. But C-047 requires the reasons to include that public-dissemination documents 'cannot be work product' and that the document was not prepared by or at the direction of an attorney. Rule 26(b)(3)(A) protects materials prepared by a party's representative, not only its attorney. Drafts of documents later made public, such as briefs, can be work product. A careful memo resting on business purpose and no litigation driver could be failed by a strict judge, though most correct memos will recite the same facts.

evidence.quote: because a document intended for public dissemination cannot be work product, it was not prepared by or at the direction of an attorney, and it has no litigation nexus
This press release contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995.

authorities.proposition: Protects documents 'prepared in anticipation of litigation or for trial by or for another party or its representative (including the other party's attorney, consultant, surety, indemnitor, insurer, or agent).'

findings.suggested_fix: Require the core reasons (non-lawyer PR author, prepared for public relations rather than because of litigation) and drop the categorical rules.

findings.title: Dual-purpose criteria impose a '90%+ / single sentence' test and forbid an all-High rating
findings.explanation: A primary- or predominant-purpose analysis for #044, #119 and #156 is appropriate. But C-031 requires a 'Third Circuit dominant purpose test' and an explanation that 90%+ business content means business dominance. Neither a numeric threshold nor that label is a settled Third Circuit formulation. C-073 then fails a list that rates all three High without acknowledging arguability, although C-031's own framing makes them clearly deficient. C-073 also grades against the unrequested risk scale. A memo that correctly recommends redacting the single legal sentence and producing the rest is left in between.

evidence.quote: explains that when 90%+ of a communication is business and only a single sentence requests legal input, the dominant purpose is business
FAIL if they are all rated High with no acknowledgment of arguability

findings.suggested_fix: Accept any correct articulation of the primary/predominant purpose test and any reasoned severity or redaction recommendation.

findings.title: Attributes a three-element log-content rule (subject matter, attorney, nature of advice) to Rule 26(b)(5)(A)
findings.explanation: Rule 26(b)(5)(A) requires the party to expressly claim privilege and describe the withheld items so others can assess the claim. The 'attorney involved' and 'nature of advice' elements are a case-law gloss that fits ACP but not work-product entries such as #168 (logged WP). A memo that accurately states the rule's assessability standard may fail if it omits the three items.

evidence.quote: privilege logs must identify the subject matter, the attorney involved, and the nature of the advice sought or given

authorities.proposition: Withholding party must expressly make the claim and describe the nature of the materials in a manner that will enable other parties to assess the claim.

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo explains that descriptions must give enough information (author/recipient roles, subject matter, basis) for the opposing party to assess the claim.

findings.title: Record says Reese had a counsel-coordinated litigation engagement, undercutting 'no protection arrangement' and a fixed High rating for #078
findings.explanation: C-021 requires stating that Graystone had no privilege-protection arrangement, and C-072 requires #078 and #102 to be High. Marsh's email and the Pacific Mutual CIA support a waiver finding. But the expert disclosure says Reese has had a separate litigation-support engagement 'coordinated through Carrick, Lowe & Marsh LLP' since 2020, which is before the June 2021 forward. A careful memo could argue Reese was counsel's agent, or that work product survives because Graystone and the Ridgeline broker are not adversaries, and rate #078 or #102 Medium. #128 (disclosure to NJDEP) is clearly highest-tier.

evidence.quote: Additional compensation for litigation-related expert services has been provided since 2020 under a separate litigation support engagement coordinated through Carrick, Lowe & Marsh LLP.
absent a common interest agreement or other privilege-preserving arrangement, disclosure of our legal strategy or analysis to their team could constitute a waiver
FAIL if any waiver entry is rated Medium or Low.

findings.suggested_fix: Reconcile the expert disclosure with sample-doc-078. Require #128 to be highest-tier, and accept High or Medium for #078 and #102 with a reasoned waiver analysis.

findings.title: Distractor #025's log date conflicts with its document date, inviting a flag that C-064 penalizes
findings.explanation: C-064 fails any answer that flags #025, #039 or #050 as deficient. #025 is logged April 10, 2020, but its sample is dated April 10, 2019. Privilege holds either way because Langford was GC from March 15, 2019. Still, C-057 and C-058 reward catching log date errors, so a diligent reviewer who lists #025 for log correction may be judged to have flagged a deficiency.

evidence.quote: **Date:** April 10, 2019

findings.suggested_fix: Fix the date, or clarify that a metadata correction is not a 'privilege deficiency' for C-064.

findings.title: 'Clawback candidate list' is a misnomer for a list of withheld entries with deficient claims
findings.explanation: In practice, a clawback list identifies privileged documents that were produced and should be retrieved under FRE 502 or a protective order. The rubric instead expects the list to contain withheld log entries whose claims fail. Some samples carry 'DOCUMENT PRODUCTION' headers, which supports the literal reading. A solver using standard usage could build the opposite list and fail C-080, with knock-on effects on C-069 and C-082, which are flagged elsewhere.

evidence.quote: **PRINTED EMAIL CORRESPONDENCE --- DOCUMENT PRODUCTION**
Output: `deficiency-analysis-memo.docx` and `clawback-candidate-list.xlsx`.

findings.suggested_fix: Rename the file (e.g., challenged-entries-list.xlsx), or state in the instructions that it lists log entries with deficient privilege claims.

findings.title: Crime-fraud flag and mandatory escalation for #072 rest on a request for advice about whether delay is lawful
findings.explanation: In #072, Pruitt asks for legal advice on 'any legal basis for holding off', and Langford warns against delay. Nothing in the record shows the report was delayed or that the advice furthered a crime or fraud. Asking whether conduct is lawful is core privileged advice. C-052 and C-081 are hedged ('potentially', 'special handling') and a cautious 'confirm the report was timely filed' note would pass. But a memo that correctly concludes the exception does not apply may fail both, and would then fail C-082 when #072 is left off the list.

evidence.quote: Is there any legal basis for holding off until we have a better handle on the remediation plan?
Delayed reporting could buy us time to assess the scope of the exceedance and develop a remediation framework before NJDEP gets involved, but it carries significant enforcement risk.
FAIL if Entry #072 is treated the same as routine deficiencies with no special handling recommendation.

findings.suggested_fix: Accept either a conditional crime-fraud risk flag or a reasoned conclusion that the exception does not apply on this record.

findings.title: C-063 states that all materials a testifying expert considered lose work-product protection
findings.explanation: Flagging #199 is correct (C-062): the disclosure lists the March 22, 2022 report as considered. But C-063 requires explaining that 'materials considered by the expert lose or have substantially diminished' protection. Rule 26(b)(4)(B)-(C) still protects draft reports and attorney-expert communications, except those about compensation, facts or data, or assumptions. A nuanced memo will usually pass, but the criterion rewards the overbroad rule.

evidence.quote: materials considered by the expert lose or have substantially diminished work product protection
Technical report on contamination migration patterns dated March 22, 2022, prepared by Dr. Reese at the direction of Carrick, Lowe & Marsh LLP.

authorities.proposition: Drafts of Rule 26(a)(2) reports and communications between a party's attorney and a reporting expert remain protected, except communications relating to compensation, identifying facts or data provided and considered, or identifying assumptions relied on.

findings.suggested_fix: Require explanation that facts/data considered and the final report are discoverable, while acknowledging draft and attorney-communication protections.

final.changes_from_blind: Dropped blind O12 (record anachronisms, C-078 and C-062). Using the January 15, 2024 disclosure date still passes, so I no longer treat those criteria as defective. I note the anachronisms only as background. Revised O3 to cover C-082 only: C-080 is sound on its own and is now arguable only through the 'clawback' label (O11). Split blind O4: C-069 and C-070 stay problematic, and C-073 moves to the dual-purpose finding (O7) with C-031. Revised O6 (C-047) to add Sol's point that Rule 26(b)(3)(A), which I read this session, does not require attorney preparation. I kept it arguable rather than Sol's 'confirmed', because correct memos will naturally recite the same facts. Revised O9 after reading Sol's F06: the expert disclosure says Reese has had a CLM-coordinated litigation-support engagement since 2020, which makes C-021 arguable and strengthens the C-072 concern. Adopted from Sol: O12 (C-052, C-081 crime-fraud; my earlier notes already raised it) and O13 (C-063 expert-materials overbreadth). Rejected Sol's F05 (common interest), because Garfield CIA §7.2 disclaims any prior informal agreement. Also rejected F04's challenge to the boilerplate criteria C-037 to C-044. I kept C-010 problematic, whereas Sol rated it arguable.
final.overall: Most of the issue-spotting rubric is sound and well grounded in the record: the non-lawyer, Molina, pre-GC, pre-engagement, boilerplate, impossible-date, board-package and NJDEP-waiver criteria. Five defects can zero out a correct answer under all-pass scoring. C-079 requires a deadline that is not in the record. C-056 requires a misstatement of the former-employee Upjohn rule. C-082's two-way presence test punishes any reasoned clearance of a planted entry. C-069 and C-070 impose an unrequested column schema and risk scale. C-010 builds in an irrelevant rationale for a message sent to the General Counsel. Sol and I agree on C-079 and C-056. We differ in degree on C-047 and C-064 (Sol confirmed, I say arguable) and on C-010 (I say problematic). I reject Sol's common-interest and boilerplate findings on record evidence. The remaining arguable items are overbroad legal rationales (C-046, C-047, C-063), fixed risk tiers (C-072, C-073), the crime-fraud handling of #072 (C-052, C-081), a record tension about Reese's engagement (C-021), and the misleading 'clawback' filename.
